title: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
hookLine: God buries Moses, and no one knows his grave to this day

cards: Pyramids. Mausoleums. A marble tomb with a line of visitors outside.
Well-known people are often given well-known graves, and pilgrims travel far to stand where a founder lies, leaving flowers, candles, notes, stones. Some tombs become places of prayer.
Moses, the teacher at the center of the Torah, dies on a mountain in Moab. And the text goes out of its way to tell us there is nothing to visit.

teach.h: MOSES DIES IN THE LAND OF MOAB.
teach.b: So Moses, the servant of God, dies there in the land of Moab, at God's word.
He is buried in a valley opposite Beth-peor, the text says, "and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Who buried him? The Hebrew simply says: he buried him.
Rashi says it was God, in His glory. The Talmud, in Sotah, takes that seriously and turns it into a teaching about how people should live. God clothed Adam and Eve.
God visited Abraham when he was healing. God comforted Isaac when he mourned. And God buried Moses.

So, the Talmud says, walk in God's ways: clothe, visit, comfort, bury. When volunteers of a chevra kadisha, a Jewish burial society, care for the body of someone who has died, they're walking in that line.
And the hidden grave? The text doesn't say why. One explanation often given is that the people would have made it a place of worship, and Moses had always pointed beyond himself.
Whatever the reason, the effect is clear.
No shrine. No relic. What remains of Moses is what he taught.
And the teaching isn't left in one place. It's in each Torah scroll, read aloud week by week. Moses' grave is unknown.
His words are read wherever the scroll is opened.

how: Jewish tradition calls caring for the dead chesed shel emet, a true kindness, since it can't be repaid; local chevra kadisha societies prepare bodies for burial, and tradition places Moses' death on the 7th of Adar, a day some burial societies mark.

o: and this is the end: the Torah's final verse
and this is the blessing: the last Torah portion
and this is the grave: where Moses was buried

games.q: inside the burial — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah says where Moses is buried
'no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day'.
the Talmud learns from Moses' burial that people should bury the dead

games.q: Moses has died, and a grave could easily become a shrine. what does the Torah's account do?
o: describe the grave so it can be marked.
say no one knows where he lies.
carry his body into the land.
games.why: 'no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day': no shrine, only the teaching.

practice: Think of someone who has died whose words or habits still live in you, a grandmother's saying, a teacher's correction, a friend's way of laughing at trouble, and name one thing they taught you.
Then think of one thing you'd like to pass on in the same way, so that it outlasts you.

wordCard.voice: V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. A portion that ends with a death, an unknown grave, and a teaching that stays.

orig.note: Hebrew: teaching, instruction. what remains of Moses when no one knows his grave.
